title: Request Cancellation and Graceful Shutdown
description: Use CancellationToken to propagate request cancellation, implement graceful shutdown patterns, and ensure in-flight work completes safely before the application stops.

data.text: In production, requests do not always run to completion. A user may close a browser tab, a load balancer may drop an idle connection, or an orchestrator may signal that the application is shutting down. **Request cancellation** in ASP.NET Core uses `CancellationToken` to propagate these signals through your code so you can stop work early and release resources cleanly.

Graceful shutdown is the companion concept. When the host receives a stop signal, it stops accepting new requests and gives in-flight requests a limited window to finish. If your code respects cancellation tokens, the application can drain active work and shut down without losing data or corrupting state.

ASP.NET Core binds several `CancellationToken` sources to each request. The most important is `HttpContext.RequestAborted`, which is triggered when the client disconnects. Additional tokens come from the host lifetime during shutdown. You should pass these tokens all the way down to `async` APIs like EF Core queries, HTTP calls, and `Task.Delay`.

data.text: When a stop signal arrives, the host begins a coordinated shutdown. It stops accepting new requests, triggers the `IApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping` event, waits for the shutdown timeout, and then exits. Your middleware, controllers, and hosted services must observe cancellation to participate in this graceful flow.

data.title: Graceful shutdown sequence
items: Host receives SIGTERM, Ctrl+C, or IIS stop signal.
Kestrel stops accepting new TCP connections.
IHostedService.StopAsync is called with a timeout token.
If work completes within ShutdownTimeout, the process exits cleanly.
If the timeout expires, the host logs a warning and forces exit.

data.title: Do Not Block Shutdown Indefinitely
data.text: StopAsync should complete quickly. If you perform long cleanup work, such as draining a large queue, use the cancellation token to stop accepting new work and finish only the items already in progress. The default ShutdownTimeout is five seconds.

`BackgroundService` automatically passes a cancellation token to `ExecuteAsync`. Use this token to break out of loops, cancel pending async operations, and dispose resources. Never ignore this token — if you do, the host may wait indefinitely and then force-kill your process, which can lead to data loss.

data.title: Cancellation and Shutdown Summary
points: CancellationToken propagates client disconnects and host shutdown signals.
Pass HttpContext.RequestAborted to async APIs like EF Core and HttpClient.
Graceful shutdown stops new requests and lets in-flight work finish.
IHostedService.StopAsync receives a timeout token for cleanup.
BackgroundService provides ExecuteAsync with automatic cancellation support.
Always handle OperationCanceledException to exit loops cleanly.
data.takeaway: Cancellation and graceful shutdown are the safety nets of production ASP.NET Core applications. By respecting tokens throughout your codebase, you ensure that requests can be abandoned safely and applications can shut down without data loss or corruption.
